descriptionChirho: Qal stem active sense of writing, composing, or recording text onto a surface (tablets, scrolls, letters, books); includes all Qal finite forms (perfect, imperfect, imperative, consecutive), infinitives, infinitive absolute, and conjunctive forms. Arabic consistently uses kataba (كَتَبَ), Korean uses both girokada (기록하다, record/chronicle) and sseuda (쓰다, write), Swahili uses -andika. This covers the entire range of active writing regardless of person, number, gender, or tense inflection.

Qal passive participle (katub/ketubim) used as a stative adjective meaning 'written' or 'recorded,' describing texts, laws, or words that stand in a written state; includes absolute and construct forms, with and without the article, and the formulaic kakkatuv ('as written') references to authoritative texts. Arabic uses maktub (مَكْتُوب) in all its case/gender inflections, Korean uses girokdoen (기록된, that which is recorded), Swahili uses the passive -andikwa with various noun class prefixes.

Nifal stem passive sense indicating the dynamic process of being written, being recorded, or being inscribed by an external agent, as opposed to the stative Qal passive participle which describes an existing written state. Arabic uses the internal passive kutiba (كُتِبَ), Korean uses girokdoeda (기록되다, be recorded) and sseuyeojida (쓰여지다, be written), Swahili uses passive -andikwa with tense markers indicating process rather than state.

Piel intensive stem and Qal/Piel active participles used substantively to denote professional writers, scribes, or those engaged in official/professional writing activity; the Piel intensifies the action to signify habitual or official composition. Arabic uses al-katibina (الْكَاتِبِينَ, the scribes/writers) and katabu (كَتَبُوا, they write officially), Korean uses girokaneun jadeul (기록하는 자들, those who record), Swahili uses -naoandika (those who write) and wanaandika (they are writing).

labelChirho: Qal: register, enroll in a list
descriptionChirho: Specialized sense of writing as registering or enrolling persons in an official list, census, or registry, distinct from composing text; the focus is on inscribing names into a register rather than authoring content. Arabic uses fi al-maktubina (فِي الْمَكْتُوبِينَ, among those registered) and inda kitabati (عِنْدَ كِتَابَةِ, at the time of registering), Korean uses girokdoen jadeul (기록된 자들, the registered ones), Swahili uses walioandikwa (those who were registered).

Nominal sense referring to the script or writing system of a people (ketav), as in 'according to their script'; this is the noun ketav rather than the verb, denoting the medium or system of writing itself. Arabic uses kitabatihim (كِتَابَتِهِمْ, their writing/script), Korean uses geulro (글로, in [their] script), Swahili uses maandishi-yao (their written script).

Anomalous entry parsed as 'Prep | 3ms' meaning 'for him' (lo); this does not represent a true verbal sense of katab but appears to be a misparsed prepositional fragment or tagging error. Arabic: lahu (لَهُ, for him), Korean: geuege (그에게, to him), Swahili: yeye (him).
